analytic.title: Scheduling Transactions in Real-Time Database Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: A Real-Time Database System (RTDBS) must be able to meet stringent timing constraints imposed on its transactions while maintaining database consistency and maximizing transaction concurrency. Our goal in this paper is to propose a new real-time database model and to introduce an efficient test for determining transaction feasibility. Given the current configuration of the database and the characteristics of the newly arrived transaction, the feasibility test cm determine a priori whether the new transactioii can be completed by its specified deadline.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: There is a growing interest in building database systems capable of meeting stringent timing constraints imposed on tr'ansactions. Unlike scheduling independent tasks in non-database systems where the computation requirements ' are usually known, the actual computation times of database transactions cannot be easily predicted. This owes to the fact that the latter can access and/or modify a large number of shared data items in main and secondary (disk) memory, and may be concurrent and prioritized, thus requiring the transactions to follow elaborate concurrency and consistency protocols which are not amenable to efficient timing analysis.

Research in real-time database systems (RTDBS) has progressed in various directions. New scheduling algorithms for I/O requests with deadlines have been developed in [3] to meet the deadlines of individuad requests by exploiting the fact that reading from the disk occurs before a transaction commits and writing to the disk usually occurs after the transaction commits. To allow transactions to meet their timing constraints as much as possible without reducing the concurrency level of the database system, new concurrency control 1063-6390/93 $3.00 0 1993 IEEE mechanisms were proposed in [ 11, [14], and [16]. Multiversion data concurrency control and priority based disk scheduling were used in [2] and [121 to further improve the RTDBS performance in terms of transaction timeliness. A conditional priority inheritance protocol for real-time databases which require a priori knowledge of the transactions' lengths as well as the number of steps each transaction has been executed was introduced in [l 1). Techniques for meeting deadlines as much :is possible of triggered transactions in order to make the database consistent were discussed in [ 131. However, we are not aware of any results which determine a priori whether a set of transactions, or an arriving trarisaction together with the transactions resident in the database, can be scheduled without missing any of their deadlines and without first acquiring all resources needed. We call this problem the trunsuction feusibility problem. Buchmann's approach [4] resembles ours but it assumes that all resources are secured by each transaction before it st2u'ts execution.

In ai RTDBS, as in other real-time system, it priori knowledge of the system's ability to meet the deadlines of the transactions can be as important as the system's ability to maximize the number of transactions which can complete before their deadlines. For instance, in certain applications, the knowledge about the (in)feasibility of the current set of transactions allows the top-level manager to select an alternate set of less computationally-demanding transactions. This knowledge is especially imponmt in real-time rulebased expert systems [SI, [6], [7], and in real-time coiltrol systems [lS] which frequently access 11 large mount of ilems in ;t knowledge base or a database. These real-time systems contain a top-level planner which can select at each meta planning step a transaction among several candidate transactions with different computational demands and qualities in order to ensure that the selected transaction's deadline can be met by the current computing power and resources of the RTDBS. Therefore, our goal in this paper is to introduce an efficient test for transaction feasibility.

The rest of this paper is organized ILS follows. Sec-tion 2 provides the motivation for our approach and introduces the RTDBS model used in this study. Section 3 defines the transaction feasibility problem. In section 4, an efficient test for transaction feasibility based on a quick transaction check algorithm and a dynamic scheduling game representation is described. Section 5 describes an example illustrating the proposed approach. Section 6 contains concluding remarks.

div.head: The Real-Time Database Model
div.p: A program is a sequence of instructions each of which can be a 'lock x', an 'unlock x', or a simple instruction which does not access a lock, where x is a data item in the database and the 1ocWunlock can be of type 'read' or type 'write'. An instruction is said to be independent if its execution time is independent of the execution of other instructions. An instruction whose execution time is dependent of the execution of other instructions is said to be dependent. Thus, a luck instruction is a dependent instruction whereas an unlock instruction or a simple instruction is an independent instruction. A program can be represented by a linear directed graph whose nodes, with the exception of the initial node and the final node, correspond to lock or unlock instructions, and the edges correspond to sequences of instructions between adjacent nodes. A segment is defined as a sequence of instructions between two adjacent nodes. Thus a segment cain be one of the following three sequences of instructions: ( I the instructions between the beginning of the program and the first lock instruction, (2) the instructions between an instruction accessing a lock atid a consecutive instruction accessing a lock, and (3) the instructions between the last unlock instruction and the end of the program.

We consider a main memory database system with multiprocessors which allow non-conflicting concurrent transactions to access and modify data item in the database. div.head: The Transaction Feasibility Problem
div.p: Given a real-time, main-memory-resident, database system with a multiprocessor CPU, transactions with completion deadlines arrive randomly to be processed by the database scheduler. If two or more transactions arrive at exactly the same time, they are placed in a queue according to their deadlines with the one having the nearest deadline placed at the head of the queue, and then processed by the scheduler as if they arrive at different times. Ties are broken arbitrarily for transactions whose deadlines are the same. When a transaction arrives, the scheduler performs a feasibility test to determine whether the arriving transaction can complete its execution by its specified deadline without affecting the feasibility of my of the transactions already resident in the datiibase. A transaction is said to be feusible if (1) it can be scheduled and completed by its specified deadline without preempting any of the resident transactions or (2) it can be scheduled by preempting one or more of the resident transactions with the constraint that all deadlines of these to-bepreempted resident transactions are still met. Here, "to preempt a transaction T," may mean (1) to abort T; if T, has executed a write lock and has held the lock, or
( 2 ) to temporarily suspend T, and resume it from the point at which T, is preempted.

In our approach, even if the arriving transaction has ;iii earlier deadline than some of those transactions resident in the system, the arriving transaction should not preempt other transactions if the new and the resident transactions can still be completed prior to their respective deadlines without preemption. This approach is chosen to minimize the amount of wasted processor time spent in executing transactions which will be aborted. If the deadline of the arriving transaction can be met only by preempting one or more resident transactions, then it is allowed to do so only if the deadlines of the resident transactions whose deadlines have Leady been guaranteec to be met are still satisfied. This ensures the following: when the scheduler decides that a transaction is feasible, then its deadline should be met regardless of the behavior of future transactions. Thus the 2PL-EDP protocol used in our model is more appropriately termed 2PLconditional earliest deadline priority (2PL-CEDP).

div.head: The Database Scheduler and an Efficient Feasibility Test
div.p: The database scheduler consists of a runtime monitoring facility aid a transaction feasibility tester. The runtime monitoring facility monitors the progress of every resident transaction which has not completed its execution and updates the corresponding database system parameters for each transaction at each time quantum. The feasibility test for deciding whether a newly arrived transaction T, can complete by its specified deadline must take into account the total time the trm- saction is blocked and/or suspended in addition to the nominal execution time of the transaction. The test consists of two phases. The first phase derives the actual execution time of T, by considering its nominal execution time and the remaining actual execution times of the resident transactions whose lock instructions may conflict with those in T, . The second phase exploits a scheduling game representation to efficiently determine whether the arriving transaction can meet its deadline while still meeting the deadlines of all resident transactions based on the actual execution time of T, computed in phase one. The first phase of the feasibil-ity test consists of the following algorithm. The first part of the algorithm (line 1 to line 17) calculates w, , pi, U;, and Ai by considering transactions with at least one lock instruction which is in conflict with a lock in Ti. The algorithm needs only consider the transaction (with a conflicting lock) which has the latest arrival time among all transactions with conflicting locks since the waiting tune for the lock in each transaction is calculated based on previously arrived transactions. Note that transaction Ti must wait for wir time units before attempting to acquire a lock on x to allow resident transactions whose deadlines have been guaranteed to be met to acquire a lock on n first. Otherwise, a resident transaction certified as feasible may miss its deadline if the lock 011 x is acquired first by Ti. During actual execution, the w; of a transaction T', is used to determine whether T; should wait before requesting a lock on a item x even if no locking conflicts exist yet. This is to ensure that an earlier transaction Ti which has in it a lock request for item x but which has not yet executed the instruction 'lock x ' to acquire that lock first before T,. This approach guarantees that a resident transaction will meet its deadline regardless of the behavior of future transactions admitted into the database. The code segment at line 10 and line 11 are needed to assign the correct value (0) to wiJ if T, has released the conflicting lock (if read lock) or Tj has committed (if write lock) before Ti requests a lock on item x .

div.head: Computing Actual Computation Times of Transactions
div.p: If the estimated actual execution time of the arriving transaction Ti computed in the first part exceeds the transaction's deadline, the second part of the algorithm (line 18 to line 32) is used to determine whether the preeinption of one or more resident transactions which have lower priority (less urgent deadlines) and which has at least one lock in conflict with a lock in Ti allows Ti to complete its execution by its deadline. Note that in calculating the sum of the lock-waiting times w,,'s, we only consider the read locks in the instructions of T, which have not been executed and these locks conflict with those in Ti. However, for conflicting write locks, we need to consider all executing transactions with such locks. Preemption is allowed only if all resident transactions will still be able to complete execution by their respective deadlines. Therefore, if one T, has been found to miss its deadline if preempted by Ti, the algorithm terminates by indicating the transaction is not feasible. Otherwise, all computed parameters of all other T,s must he recalculated, which may be complicated and computationally expensive.

div.head: Determining Transaction Feasibility
div.p: The second phase of the feasibility test makes use of the following scheduling game representation. A scheduling problem with m independent tasks and n processors (m > n ) can be formulated in the form of a scheduling game [8]. In pruticular, the remaining computation times and the laxities of the tasks at any instance of time can be represented by the placement of tokens on a scheduling game board. The status of each task which has arrived can be characterized by two parameters: the remaining computation time C(i) at time i and the deadline D ( i ) by which to complete it. The laxity measures the urgency of a ask at time i and it is defined by: L ( i ) = D (i) -C(i). The scheduling problem at time i is represented by a configuration of tokens in the first quadrant of a Cartesian plane with the vertical axis C representing remaining computation time and the horizontal axis L representing laxity.

For convenience, the set of rules goveming the movement of tokens are repeated below.
(1) The scheduler is provided with an initial configuration of m tokens in the first quadrant of a Cartesian game board (the L -C plane).

( 2 ) At each step of the game, the scheduler is allowed to move at most n of the tokens one division downwards towards the horizontal axis. The rest of the tokens must be moved one division to the left towards the vertical axis.

(3) Any token reaching the horizontal axis can be ignored for the rest of the game (its deadline has been met). ( 4) The scheduler fails if any token crosses the vertical axis into the second quadrant of the Cartesim game board before reaching the horizorital axis.
( 5 ) The scheduler wins (achieves scheduling) if in a succession of steps all tokens are evacuated without incurring failure.

div.head: Concluding Remarks
div.p: We have described an efficient algorithm for determining the feasibility of a transaction with runtime linearly proportional to the number of lock requests in the transaction. The schedulability checker based on the game board representation determines trarisaction schedulability one at a time (incrementally) and thus it dso has linea runtime complexity once the checker is initialized. We are currently investigating the practicality of this approach by simulation and by actual implementation on a network of RISC workstations. A guideline for practical graceful degradation by means of a monitor/filter for incoming transactions is also being developed. Future work will integrate this RTDBS and its scheduler with a real-time rule-based expert system to yield a hard real-time knowledgedatabase system.
